payload.system: Return only the requested structured result. Act as a skeptical but fair reader and compare the book with the strongest specific alternative explanation.

messages.content:
You are the skeptical-reader judge in the final stage of a blinded experiment.
Independent agents have already found that the book's conclusion diverges from
a recognizable common interpretation. Your task is comparative: after reading
the book's sources and full argument, determine which specific interpretation
best explains the supplied scriptural evidence.

TERM
Valley

COMMON INTERPRETATION
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the valley most commonly symbolizes a season of trial, suffering, darkness, or spiritual low point — the 'low place' of human experience (often contrasted with mountaintop experiences of blessing or divine encounter) through which God nevertheless accompanies and sustains the believer.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Psalm 23:4 (the valley of the shadow of death — God's presence in the darkest place)",

      "prominence": "common"

Nevertheless, in popular Christian teaching, hymnody, and devotional literature there is a strong, recognizable convention: the valley stands for the dark or difficult season of life traversed with God, driven above all by Psalm 23:4. The judgment-valley (Joel/Hinnom) and restoration-valley (Ezekiel 37) readings are well established but are usually treated as context-specific rather than as the default symbolic meaning."

Biblical studies, however, does not treat valley as having one fixed symbolic meaning. BOOK ENTRY
The low and humbled — the opposite of the mountain-kingdom; “every valley shall be exalted”.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 40:4) · see Mountain, ch. 39 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 40:4 — Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/39-mountain.adoc

The first case study is “mountain,” which represents kingdoms or power structures.
The pyramid-like structure of a mountain mirrors the power structure of delegated authority and is an apt analogy — but subjective aptness is not a basis for defining a symbol.
Thankfully, in this case Scripture comes right out and defines it:

This calls for a mind with wisdom.
The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits.
They are also seven kings (kingdoms).

Revelation tells us that mountains mean kingdoms, and by analogy hills are cities.
The question is whether Scripture consistently uses mountain with the same symbolic meaning, or whether this is a one-off.
Other times in Scripture we are given a vision and an interpretation, which establishes the definition by analogy:

Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were crushed together, and became like chaff from the summer threshing floors; the wind carried them away so that no trace of them was found.
And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
Inasmuch as you saw that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold — the great God has made known to the king what will come to pass after this.
The dream is certain, and its interpretation is sure.

In this case Daniel explains a vision of a statue with layers of gold, silver, bronze, and feet of clay and iron, and explains that this statue represents successive kingdoms.
Then a final kingdom comes and destroys the statue and rules for ever and ever.
The final kingdom of the statue is consumed when God’s kingdom comes as a stone that grows into a mountain over the entire earth.

The stone itself repays a closer look.
It is “cut out… without hands” (Daniel 2:45) — and to cut is the covenant verb (Genesis 15:18). [Footnote: Covenants are cut, not made — karath — as the Daniel Unsealed chapter showed.]
A stone cut by no human hand is a covenant cut by God Himself — and Scripture names the Rock: “that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), the covenant in person; “the stone which the builders refused” is become “the head stone of the corner” (Psalm 118:22).
So the stone and the rock are the covenant, and the mountain it grows into is that covenant become a kingdom over all the earth.

You are this head of gold.
After you shall arise another kingdom inferior to yours; then another, a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth.

The fact that the mountain is described as growing and covering the entire earth is another clue that this isn’t a physical mountain.
The analogy from Daniel is carried on in Isaiah.

It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come.

See the same symbolic meaning applied in Jeremiah, describing Babylon the Great, which rules over the whole earth and destroys nation after nation.
Here Jeremiah tells us this destroying mountain will become a burnt mountain.

“Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, Who destroys all the earth,” says the Lord.
“And I will stretch out My hand against you, Roll you down from the rocks, And make you a burnt mountain.”

Now we have Daniel, Revelation, Isaiah, and Jeremiah all agreeing on the meaning of this symbol of a Mountain as a Kingdom.
With this knowledge we can now gain greater insight into many other scriptures.
Consider the account in Revelation of a flaming mountain thrown into the sea:

Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a huge mountain, all ablaze, was thrown into the sea.
A third of the sea turned into blood, a third of the living creatures in the sea died….

To gauge how this verse is usually read, I asked Claude, as before, to name the most common explanations of this “mountain” and estimate how prevalent each one is.
By this estimate, about 85% miss the symbolic meaning here:

.How the “mountain” is usually read (Rev. 8:8)

|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | Literal asteroid or meteor impact | 40%
| 2 | Literal volcano hurled into the sea | 25%
| 3 | Nuclear blast or modern warfare | 20%
| 4 | A nation or world empire | 15%
|===

How do we know that this isn’t a literal mountain in this context?
The answer is in the phrase “thrown into the sea,” the “sea turning into blood,” and the “creatures in the sea,” all in the same sentence.
In a later chapter I will show the evidence that sea is a symbol that means the masses of people, the population of the earth, and that living creatures, beast, and animals represent gentile nations.

Symbolically, Revelation 8:8-9 is saying that when a “huge mountain” — a world empire — is thrown down, a third of the people will die and a third of the nations will be destroyed.
This implies that on the order of two billion people will die when this mountain is thrown down.

One final supporting piece of evidence is that a “stone, rock, mountain, etc.” being “thrown into the sea” to “never rise again” is the prophetic symbol tied to the fall of Babylon the Great.
And thus symbols can be composed of both words and catch-phrases.

So Jesus said to them, “Because of your unbelief; for assuredly, I say to you, if you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.”

So Jesus answered and said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but also if you say to this mountain, ‘Be removed and be cast into the sea,’ it will be done.”

For assuredly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be removed and be cast into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that those things he says will be done, he will have whatever he says.

Once again I asked Claude to rank how this “mountain” is understood, and a national power sits at the very bottom of the list — so low it barely registers:

.How the “mountain” Jesus moves is usually read

|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | A personal obstacle or problem | 55%
| 2 | A literal mountain (hyperbole) | 25%
| 3 | The Mount of Olives / Temple Mount | 8%
| 4 | A spiritual stronghold or doubt | 6%
| 5 | The corrupt temple/religious system | 4%
| 6 | A national power or kingdom | 2%
|===

How do we know that this mountain is not a literal mountain, or merely an impossible obstacle, in this context?
Because the context is a fig tree and a mustard tree — and trees are another symbol that Scripture defines as kingdoms or nations — and of course “thrown into the sea” is a symbol clearly referring to Babylon the Great, as the Fall of Babylon chapter demonstrated — and as the next chapter will trace from the Song of the Sea onward.

What we learn from this is that the symbolic language of the Bible is interconnected: symbols are defined in terms of symbols and phrases, as well as the verbs, adjectives, and other personifications used with the symbol.
For this reason, we often see the same set of symbols connected over and over.

Though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof.

.How the “mountains” are usually read (Ps. 46)

|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | Literal earthquakes or natural disaster | 40%
| 2 | Life’s troubles and instability | 27%
| 3 | Cosmic or end-times upheaval | 18%
| 4 | Nations or kingdoms shaken | 15%
|===

Once again, by Claude’s estimate, the symbolic meaning is missed by roughly 85% of those who interpret the verse.
Now consider this poetic picture from Joel:

A day of darkness and gloom, A day of clouds and of thick [dark] mist, Like the dawn spread over the mountains;

The picture is of “dawn,” “mist,” or “fog” spread over the “mountains,” which is quite common in early morning and aligns with the visual of a “day of clouds and thick dark mist.”
The Hebrew word for “dawn,” shachar, names the dark before sunrise. [Footnote: Derived — shachar written on the letters of blackness — in the Lucifer's Declared Plan chapter.] It names the first light while the sky is still quite dark, before the sun burns away the fog.
Now, with the greater context, we have dark clouds of smoke spread over the nations.
This is just one of dozens of verses that gain new meaning when you apply the symbolic meaning of mountain.

So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.

Here is a verse that contains instructions for the future, and to understand the instructions it is helpful to know that “mountains” means nations.
In other words: get out of Judea.
In AD 70, those who survived the fall of Jerusalem were scattered to the nations, so this prophecy has been fulfilled in this sense already.

When you see Jerusalem being surrounded by armies, you will know that its desolation is near.
Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, let those in the city get out, and let those in the country not enter the city.

Another verse sounds poetic on the surface, but carries a far more practical message when read by Scripture’s own symbols:

My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray, in the mountains they have turned them away. From mountain to hill they have gone; they have forgotten their resting place.

Here His people are the sheep; the shepherds are the pastors and teachers who led people astray among the nations they were scattered to.
His people have gone from nation to city and have forgotten their home.

Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low.

This verse from Isaiah now has far deeper meaning: the nations and cities will be humbled (brought low).
And those who are humble, obedient even to death, will be exalted and lifted up.
The mountains are high places, proud places, and they contrast with their opposite, the valleys — those enslaved by the mountains.

Behold, I will send for many fishers, said the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the holes of the rocks.

Here is another case where mountains (nations) are used with other symbols: fishermen and hunters.
Here Jeremiah is prophesying about Jesus calling people to be fishers of men.
Then, those who are not caught as fish will be hunted down from among the nations, in every city, and out of every bunker.
The holes of the rocks are then referenced in Revelation:

And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places.
And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every slave, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; and said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us.

Now that you know that mountain means a kingdom, we should ask ourselves: what does an island represent?

And great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.
And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found.

Are literal mountains going to disappear, or is this clearly talking about the third of the nations thrown into the sea, never to rise again?
When I read this, it struck me as odd that an island could flee, or escape.
It is the personification of island that led me to research the island symbol, which we will cover in a future chapter.

I will close this chapter on mountains with one final notable use, when Jesus was tested in the desert:

Again, the devil takes him up into an exceeding high mountain, and shows him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;

Here we see an exceedingly high mountain from which all the other kingdoms of the earth can be seen.
In other words, he is taken to a kingdom ruling over all the other kings of the earth — likely Babylon the Great.

By now you should see the pattern: Scripture reliably and consistently uses the word mountain as a way to say “nation” or “kingdom” in many different contexts across the whole of Scripture.
I have only addressed a few of the notable uses, but once you internalize this symbol you will find it used in countless other places in profound ways.

In the process of exploring the mountain symbol, we came across many other symbols: the sea (the masses of mankind), the hills (cities), the tree and the fig tree (kingdoms and Israel), the stone and the rock (the covenant), the beasts and living creatures (the gentile nations), the island, the fishers and the hunters, the valley, and Babylon the Great.
The sea, the trees and their beasts, and the island are taken up in the chapters just ahead, each defined the same way we defined the mountain — by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
Babylon the Great we have already traced through Part Five, and the glossary carries the rest.

A word, then, about what we have just done with AI.
Left to its own intuition, the AI missed the plain meaning of the mountain in nearly every verse — it simply returned the common teachings the tables above record.
Yet the moment it was given the process to follow, and made to follow it step by step, the same meaning became clear and all but deterministic.

The contrast matters: AI does not interpret Scripture for us, and it must not be trusted to — but the meaning is already there, recoverable by anyone, or anything, willing to follow the method rather than lean on inherited opinion.
What forces the right answer is not the cleverness of the reader but the discipline of the process.
